title: How ‘inevitable’ is World War Three?
summary: Two defence analysts weigh the odds of a world war in the next decade, a Taiwan trigger, and whether Russia could attack the Baltic states.

assertions.quote: a Chinese invasion of Taiwan is, I still think probably the most likely single cause of a major global conflict.

verdicts.note: Most analysts see Taiwan as the likeliest flashpoint for a US-China war, but an invasion itself remains unlikely in the near term.

Among the 40% of surveyed strategists who expect another world war within a decade, 43% named Taiwan or the East/South China Seas as the likely trigger, ahead of Eastern Europe (25%) and the Middle East (13%).

CSIS: Taiwan 'is widely regarded as the most dangerous potential flashpoint for conflict between the United States and China'; this supports Taiwan as the top US-China trigger, not as the trigger of a world war.

assertions.quote: I think it is incredibly likely that Russia would simultaneously go onto the offensive to grab the bits of NATO territory

verdicts.note: This is a claim about Russian intentions in a hypothetical, which no public record can show.

DDIS says Russia's willingness to confront European NATO states would rise if the US shifted to the Indo-Pacific, and that a Taiwan war would reduce US ability to help Europe; heightened risk, not a predicted attack.

assertions.quote: the ability of Russia to fight against NATO or European is very limited
both of the point of both of those numbers is it probably won't happen

verdicts.note: The community gives a world war 22% over about 30 years (roughly 1% a year) and lists the post-WWII de-escalation trend (globalisation, nuclear deterrence) as a key factor lowering it.
Kroenig notes zero great-power wars in the eighty years since 1945.

Clauset: a constant-hazard model gives about a 43% chance of a WWII-sized war per century, small in any one year, but the long peace since 1945 is not statistically distinguishable from chance, so the 'has become rare' part is not shown.

Cunen et al. find a significant drop in interstate war sizes around 1950 (upper quartile 63,545 to 14,943 battle deaths), supporting fewer large wars after WWII, though the timing of the change is uncertain.
Braumoeller finds that the post-WWII decline in war's deadliness is within normal variation and could be luck, with no long-term downward trend apart from a drop in initiation after the Cold War.
OWID: conflict deaths in recent decades are below most of the 20th century and relations between countries have grown more peaceful, but the future of the trend is uncertain.

Hanania observes that the GDP power shifts of recent decades (China relative to Japan and Russia, Germany within Europe) brought no war, and that the disappearance of interstate conflict suggests power transitions no longer carry the risk of war they once did.
Metaculus notes no World War III as of 2024 despite close calls, and its 'World War Three before 2050?' question (3.3k forecasters, in the sidebar) stands at 22%, roughly 1% a year.

assertions.quote: with using hybrid tool he will fight again Europe but not with kinetic tools
Russia could mount a very limited operation into NATO territory to say grab a city like Narva

verdicts.note: European defence officials warn of this scenario, but Russia has not attacked NATO territory and NATO's forward forces raise the cost.
DDIS judges Russia could be ready for a local war against a neighbour within about six months of the Ukraine war ending, if NATO appears divided; capability with conditions, not a stated plan.

assertions.quote: I say that the deterrence is coming from the UK and the French and not from the US

verdicts.note: Whether a US president would honour Article 5 is a question of intent that no public record settles.
